nameStory: The American persimmon gets its name from 'putchamin,' an Algonquian word meaning 'dry fruit,' which European settlers adapted into 'persimmon.' This perfectly captures the fruit's puckering, mouth-drying effect when eaten before it's fully ripe - a mistake you'll only make once!
description: The American persimmon is a medium-sized native tree that can grow 30-60 feet tall with a rounded crown. It's famous for its orange, plum-sized fruits that ripen in fall, transforming from astringent mouth-puckerers to sweet, honey-like treats. The tree has distinctive dark, blocky bark and simple oval leaves that turn yellow-orange in autumn. While native to the southeastern United States, it occasionally appears in southern New England as an adventurous northern wanderer.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to nearly black bark broken into distinctive square or rectangular blocks, creating a checkerboard pattern that's unmistakable once you've seen it

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval leaves 3-6 inches long with smooth edges and a leathery feel, arranged alternately on branches with prominent parallel veins running from midrib to edge

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Orange, tomato-like fruits about 1-2 inches across that feel soft and squishy when ripe, with a sweet, almost honey-custard flavor and large brown seeds inside

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, creamy white or greenish-yellow bell-shaped flowers that appear in late spring, with male and female flowers typically on separate trees

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows in small colonies from root sprouts, creating clusters of trees, with younger trees having a more upright form than the rounded mature specimens

habitat: In New England, American persimmon is found primarily in southern Connecticut in well-drained soils along woodland edges, old fields, and disturbed areas. It prefers full sun to partial shade and adapts to various soil types but thrives in rich, loamy soils. Look for it in areas that stay relatively warm and protected from harsh winter winds.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous bell-shaped flowers appear in late May to early June after leaves have emerged, with male and female flowers on separate trees.
seasonality.summer: Full green foliage provides good shade, and small green fruits begin developing on female trees, though they're hard and very astringent if tasted.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant yellow-orange, and fruits ripen to orange, becoming soft and sweet after the first frost - this is prime harvest time for both humans and wildlife.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the distinctive blocky bark pattern most clearly, and persistent fruits may hang on the tree, providing important winter food for animals.

funFact: Native Americans used persimmon seeds to predict winter weather - they'd crack open the seed to look at the shape inside, believing it would show whether the coming winter would bring lots of snow, ice, or mild weather!
confusionNotes: The distinctive blocky bark is unique and prevents confusion with most other trees. However, young persimmons with smoother bark might be confused with cherry or dogwood trees, but persimmon leaves are larger and have more prominent parallel veining running straight from the midrib to the leaf edge.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse American persimmons with the larger, orange Asian persimmons sold in grocery stores - those come from a different species. Also, remember that most persimmon trees are either male or female, so you need both nearby to get fruit, and the fruits must be fully ripe (soft and squishy) to be edible.
compareHints: American persimmon is the only persimmon species found wild in New England, making identification easier. Within its family, it's most similar to ebony trees found in tropical regions, sharing the same hard, dense wood and simple leaves, but ebony trees don't produce the large, edible fruits that make persimmons famous.
